name: Phase 1 — Introduction & Core Trade-offs
description: The fundamental trade-offs behind every design
content:
# Phase 1: Introduction & core trade-offs

A system design interview has **no single right answer**. The interviewer checks whether you can clarify requirements, pick trade-offs, and justify them. Every later phase is a tool; this phase is the thinking behind choosing the tool.

**Java/Spring Boot angle:** you will be asked to sketch Spring Boot services, their database, cache and queue, and to say what breaks at 10x load.

name: Introduction
description: What system design is and how to approach it
content: Start here: what the interview is and a repeatable framework.

name: What is System Design?
description: Designing components, data flow and trade-offs to meet requirements at scale
content:
# What is system design?

System design = deciding **which components** (services, databases, caches, queues), **how they talk**, and **how they behave under load and failure**, so that functional and non-functional requirements are met.

**Analogy:** building a city, not a house. A house (one Spring Boot app + one DB) works for 100 people. A city needs roads (network), water supply (caching/queues), zoning (service boundaries) and emergency services (failover).

## Two kinds of requirements

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| Functional | "User can shorten a URL", "Place an order" |
| Non-functional (NFR) | 10k requests/sec, p99 < 200 ms, 99.99% availability, data never lost |

NFRs drive the architecture. A CRUD API with 10 users and one with 10 million need different designs for the *same* features.

## Monolith to scaled system (typical story)

```text
Stage 1:  Client -> Spring Boot app -> PostgreSQL          (works to ~1k RPS)
Stage 2:  + Redis cache, + read replica                    (reads scale)
Stage 3:  + Load balancer, N stateless app instances       (compute scales)
Stage 4:  + Kafka, async workers                           (spikes absorbed)
Stage 5:  + Sharding / microservices / multi-region        (data & team scale)
```
- Each stage is added only when a measured bottleneck demands it. Over-engineering is also a design failure.

## Remember
- Design is about **trade-offs**, never "best technology".
- Always tie a choice to a requirement: "I add Redis *because* reads are 100:1 vs writes."

Q: Is system design about picking popular tools?
A: No. It is about meeting requirements (scale, latency, availability, cost) with justified trade-offs. Tools are the implementation.

Q: Monolith or microservices first?
A: Usually a well-structured monolith first; split when team size, deploy independence or scaling needs justify the network and operational cost.

name: How to approach System Design?
description: A 5-step interview framework: requirements, estimation, API, high-level design, deep dive
content:
# How to approach a system design interview

Use the same framework every time (about 45 minutes):

| Step | Time | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Clarify requirements | 5 min | Features in/out of scope, users, read/write ratio, NFRs |
| 2. Estimate scale | 5 min | QPS, storage, bandwidth (back-of-envelope) |
| 3. API + data model | 5 min | Endpoints, main entities |
| 4. High-level design | 10 min | Boxes and arrows: client, LB, services, DB, cache, queue |
| 5. Deep dive + trade-offs | 15 min | Bottlenecks, sharding, failures, consistency, monitoring |

## Back-of-envelope example: URL shortener

```text
100M new URLs/month  -> ~40 writes/sec
Read:write = 100:1   -> ~4,000 reads/sec
5 years storage      -> 100M * 12 * 5 = 6B URLs * 500 B = ~3 TB
```
- Say your numbers aloud; the interviewer wants the *method*, not exact digits.

## Sketch the API in Spring Boot terms

```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/urls")
class UrlController {
    @PostMapping
    ResponseEntity<UrlDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUrlRequest req) { ... } // 201

    @GetMapping("/{code}")
    ResponseEntity<Void> redirect(@PathVariable String code) { ... }               // 302
}
```
- Writing 2-3 endpoints early proves you understand the contract before the boxes.

## Common mistakes
- Jumping to Kafka/Kubernetes before asking requirements.
- Giving one design without naming trade-offs.
- Ignoring failure ("what if the DB dies?") and monitoring.

Q: Interviewer says "design Twitter". First move?
A: Ask: which features (post, timeline, follow)? How many users/DAU? Read-heavy? Latency target? Then estimate scale, then design.

name: Core Trade-offs
description: Performance, scalability, latency, throughput, availability, consistency
content: The vocabulary every interviewer expects you to use precisely.

name: Performance vs Scalability
description: Slow for one user vs slow under load
content:
# Performance vs scalability

- **Performance problem:** the system is slow **for a single user**.
- **Scalability problem:** the system is fast for one user but **slow under heavy load**.

**Analogy:** a single cashier who is slow = performance. A fast cashier but 1000 customers and one counter = scalability.

## Vertical vs horizontal scaling

| | Vertical (scale up) | Horizontal (scale out) |
|---|---|---|
| How | Bigger machine | More machines |
| Limit | Hardware ceiling, single point of failure | Needs stateless design, LB, data partitioning |
| Cost | Expensive at the top | Cheap commodity nodes |

## Spring Boot: make the service horizontally scalable

```java
// BAD: state in the JVM, breaks when a 2nd instance appears
private final Map<String, Cart> carts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

// GOOD: state in Redis (shared), any instance can serve any request
@Service
class CartService {
    private final RedisTemplate<String, Cart> redis;
    Cart get(String userId) { return redis.opsForValue().get("cart:" + userId); }
}
```
- Local in-memory state ties a user to one instance; externalizing it (Redis/DB/JWT) lets you add instances freely.

## Remember
- Measure first (profiler, p99) to know which problem you have.
- Performance fixes: indexes, caching, fewer queries. Scalability fixes: stateless nodes, LB, sharding, async.

Q: Your API is slow for one request. Does adding servers help?
A: No. That is a performance problem (query, N+1, algorithm). More servers only help throughput under load.

name: Latency vs Throughput
description: Time per request vs requests per second
content:
# Latency vs throughput

- **Latency:** time to finish **one** request (ms).
- **Throughput:** requests (or bytes) handled **per second**.

**Analogy:** a highway. Latency = time one car needs A to B. Throughput = cars per hour. A wider road (more lanes) raises throughput but a single car is not faster.

## Percentiles, not averages

| Metric | Meaning |
|---|---|
| p50 | Half the requests are faster |
| p95 / p99 | The slow tail users actually feel |

Averages hide the tail. "avg 50 ms, p99 3 s" is a bad system.

## Little's Law (quick sizing)

```text
concurrent requests = throughput * latency
1000 req/s * 0.2 s = 200 requests in flight
```
- Tomcat default 200 threads: if latency rises to 1 s at 1000 req/s you need 1000 threads, so requests queue and latency explodes.

## Spring Boot knobs

```yaml
server:
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 200          # concurrency ceiling
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20   # DB concurrency ceiling
```
- Often the **DB pool**, not Tomcat, caps throughput. Raising threads without raising downstream capacity only moves the queue.

## Trade-off
- Batching/queues raise throughput but add latency. Synchronous direct calls lower latency but may cap throughput.

Q: How do you improve throughput without hurting latency?
A: Scale out stateless instances, cache hot reads, remove blocking I/O, size pools correctly. Avoid adding queues in the user-facing path.

name: Availability vs Consistency
description: Under a network partition you choose one
content:
# Availability vs consistency

- **Consistency:** every read sees the latest write.
- **Availability:** every request gets a (non-error) response, even if data may be stale.

When a network **partition** splits your nodes you cannot have both (see CAP next). Even without a partition there is a latency vs consistency trade-off.

## Real example: bank vs social feed

| System | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Bank transfer, inventory count | Consistency | Wrong balance or oversell is costly |
| Likes count, news feed | Availability | Slightly stale is fine, downtime is not |

## Spring Boot example: both modes in one app

```java
// Strong: one transaction, read from primary
@Transactional
public void transfer(Long from, Long to, BigDecimal amt) {
    Account a = repo.findByIdForUpdate(from);   // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
    ...
}

// Available/eventual: read from replica or cache
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public long likeCount(Long postId) { return cache.get(postId); } // may be a few seconds old
```
- Choose per use case inside the same product, not one global answer.

Q: Give a case where you deliberately choose availability.
A: Product page view counts or timeline: serve cached/stale data rather than fail; reconcile later.

name: CAP Theorem
description: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance
content: Under a network partition a distributed store must choose C or A.

name: AP - Availability + Partition Tolerance
description: Keep answering during a partition, accept stale data
content:
# AP systems

During a partition each side **keeps serving** requests, so replicas may diverge. They **reconcile later** (eventual consistency).

**Examples:** Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), Riak, DNS, Couchbase.

## How divergence is fixed
- **Last-write-wins (timestamp)**: simple, can lose writes.
- **Vector clocks / CRDTs**: detect or merge concurrent updates.
- **Read repair / anti-entropy**: replicas sync in the background.

## Spring Data Cassandra example

```java
CassandraTemplate template = ...;
template.getCqlOperations().execute(
    SimpleStatement.newInstance("INSERT INTO orders ...")
        .setConsistencyLevel(DefaultConsistencyLevel.ONE)); // fast, available, may be stale
```
- Consistency level **ONE** = answer from the nearest replica (AP behaviour). **QUORUM** moves toward CP.

## Remember
- AP fits: shopping cart, feeds, sensor data, anything where "always up" beats "always exact".

Q: Why can't you have CA in a distributed system?
A: Network partitions are unavoidable, so P is mandatory. The real choice is C or A *when a partition happens*.

name: CP - Consistency + Partition Tolerance
description: Refuse to answer rather than return stale data
content:
# CP systems

During a partition the minority side **rejects requests** (becomes unavailable) so no one reads or writes stale data.

**Examples:** ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase, MongoDB (majority writes), Redis Cluster (best effort), traditional RDBMS with sync replication.

## Quorum idea

```text
N = 3 replicas, W = 2 (write quorum), R = 2 (read quorum)
W + R > N  =>  every read overlaps the latest write  => strong consistency
```
- If only 1 node is reachable, W=2 cannot be met, so the write fails (unavailable). That is the "CP" cost.

## Spring example: fail fast instead of lying

```java
@Retryable(retryFor = TransientDataAccessException.class, maxAttempts = 3)
@Transactional
public void debit(Long id, BigDecimal amt) { ... }   // if primary unreachable, throw, never use stale replica
```
- For money, a clean error is better than a wrong balance.

## Remember
- CP fits: payments, inventory, leader election, config/coordination.

Q: Is PostgreSQL CP or AP?
A: A single-primary PostgreSQL with sync replication behaves CP: if the primary is unreachable writes fail. Async replicas serving reads give eventual (stale) reads.

name: Consistency Patterns
description: Weak, eventual and strong consistency
content: How fresh a read is after a write.

name: Weak Consistency
description: After a write, reads may or may not see it
content:
# Weak consistency

After a write, reads **might not** see it, and there is no promise when they will. Best-effort.

**Examples:** VoIP/video calls (dropped frames are not replayed), real-time games, memcached.

**Analogy:** a live TV broadcast. If you miss a second, it is gone.

## When to use
- Data loss/staleness is cheap and speed matters most.
- A cache you can rebuild: a miss just goes to the DB.

```java
// Cache that may lose entries any time: acceptable because DB is source of truth
String v = cache.get(key);
if (v == null) v = loadFromDb(key);
```

Q: Where would weak consistency be unacceptable?
A: Orders, payments, inventory: anything where losing or misreading a write costs money.

name: Eventual Consistency
description: Replicas converge given time without new writes
content:
# Eventual consistency

After a write, reads will **eventually** see it (typically milliseconds to seconds) if no new writes arrive. Replicas are updated **asynchronously**.

**Examples:** DNS, email, S3 (previously), Cassandra, DynamoDB, async DB replicas.

**Analogy:** gossip. Everyone hears the news, just not at the same instant.

## Read-your-writes problem (classic bug)

```text
User updates profile -> write to primary
Next page load       -> read from replica (lag 500 ms) -> sees OLD profile
```

## Spring Boot fix: pin reads after a write

```java
@Transactional                       // primary
public Profile update(Profile p) { return repo.save(p); }

@Transactional(readOnly = true)      // routed to replica via AbstractRoutingDataSource
public Profile get(Long id) { ... }
```
- Typical fixes: read from primary for a few seconds after a write, return the updated object in the write response, or use a session token/version.

## Remember
- With events (Kafka) the consumer side is eventually consistent by design; make handlers **idempotent**.

Q: How do you handle "I saved but I don't see it"?
A: Read-your-writes: route that user's next reads to the primary, or return fresh data from the write response and cache it client-side.

name: Strong Consistency
description: After a write, every read sees it

name: Availability Patterns
description: Fail-over and replication
content: How to stay up when machines die.

name: Fail-Over: Active - Active
description: Both nodes serve traffic; one dies, the other takes all
content:
# Active-active fail-over

Two or more nodes **all serve traffic** at the same time. If one dies the load balancer sends everything to the survivors.

```text
         +--> App A (50%) --+
Client -> LB                 +--> DB
         +--> App B (50%) --+
```

## Pros / cons
- (+) No idle hardware, instant fail-over, scales reads.
- (-) Each node must handle the **full** load alone after a failure (capacity planning).
- (-) If the nodes hold data, you need conflict resolution (hard for databases).

## Spring Boot: health-driven LB

```yaml
management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health
  endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true   # /actuator/health/liveness & readiness
```
- The LB/Kubernetes calls `/readiness`; an unhealthy instance is removed from rotation automatically.

Q: Active-active with a database?
A: Stateless app tier is easy. For the DB you need multi-master with conflict resolution or partition data by region, which is complex; many teams keep a single writer.

name: Fail-Over: Active - Passive
description: Standby takes over only when the active fails
content:
# Active-passive fail-over

One node is **active**; a **passive standby** waits. A heartbeat detects failure and the standby is promoted (VIP moves).

- **Hot standby:** already running and in sync, fail-over in seconds.
- **Cold standby:** started on demand, slow.

```text
Client -> Active (serves) ~~heartbeat~~ Passive (idle, replicating)
```

## Pros / cons
- (+) Simple, no conflict resolution.
- (-) Idle cost, small downtime window, risk of **split brain** (both think they are active) → use fencing / quorum.

## Example: PostgreSQL primary + standby

```text
Primary --WAL streaming--> Standby
Patroni / pg_auto_failover promotes standby when primary stops responding
App connects via a virtual IP or a connection string with multiple hosts:
jdbc:postgresql://db1,db2/app?targetServerType=primary
```
- The JDBC driver tries hosts until it finds the primary, so the Spring Boot app survives a promotion without code change.

Q: What is split brain and how to avoid it?
A: Two nodes both act as primary and accept writes, causing divergence. Prevent with quorum/leader election and fencing (STONITH).

name: Replication: Master - Slave
description: One writer, many read replicas

name: Replication: Master - Master
description: Multiple writers, needs conflict resolution
content:
# Master-master (multi-primary) replication

Several nodes accept **writes** and replicate to each other.

## Pros / cons
- (+) Write availability if a node dies; writes close to users in each region.
- (-) **Write conflicts** (same row updated on two masters). Needs last-write-wins, versioning or app-level merge.
- (-) Loosened consistency; harder to reason about; auto-increment ID collisions (use UUID/ULID/Snowflake).

## Conflict example

```text
t1: Master A sets price = 10
t1: Master B sets price = 12     (concurrently)
=> replicas disagree. LWW keeps the later timestamp (one update silently lost).
```

## Tip for the interview
- Prefer **single-writer per key** (partition by region/user) over true multi-master unless you must write everywhere.
- Mention clocks: LWW depends on synchronized clocks → use logical/hybrid clocks.

Q: When pick master-master?
A: Multi-region active-active writes with tolerance for eventual consistency (e.g., collaborative, shopping cart). Avoid for financial ledgers.

name: Availability in Numbers
description: The nines and how components combine
content: Translate "nines" into downtime and combine components.

name: 99.9% Availability - three 9s
description: About 8.77 hours downtime per year
content:
# Three nines (99.9%)

| Period | Allowed downtime |
|---|---|
| Per year | ~8h 46m |
| Per month | ~43m 50s |
| Per week | ~10m 5s |
| Per day | ~1m 26s |

Achievable with a **single redundant tier** and manual/slow recovery. Typical for internal tools.

## SLO vs SLA vs SLI
- **SLI:** the measurement (e.g., % of successful requests).
- **SLO:** your internal target (99.9%).
- **SLA:** the contract with penalties (usually looser than SLO).

Q: Is a planned 30-minute monthly maintenance within 99.9%?
A: Only just (43 min/month budget). Planned windows usually count unless the SLA excludes them; prefer zero-downtime deploys (rolling/blue-green).

name: 99.99% Availability - four 9s
description: About 52 minutes downtime per year
content:
# Four nines (99.99%)

| Period | Allowed downtime |
|---|---|
| Per year | ~52m 36s |
| Per month | ~4m 23s |
| Per week | ~1m 5s |

A human cannot react in 4 minutes: needs **automatic** fail-over, health checks, multi-AZ, zero-downtime deploys and no single point of failure.

## What it takes (Spring Boot service)
- N≥2 instances across availability zones behind a load balancer.
- Readiness/liveness probes + auto restart (Kubernetes).
- DB with automatic fail-over (multi-AZ), connection retry.
- Circuit breaker, timeouts and retries so a slow dependency does not take you down (Resilience4j).
- Rolling/canary deploys, backward-compatible DB migrations (Flyway).

Q: Cost of each extra nine?
A: Roughly an order of magnitude more cost and complexity. Pick the nines the business actually needs.

name: Availability in Parallel vs Sequence
description: Serial multiplies, parallel improves
content:
# Availability: sequence vs parallel

## In sequence (all must work)
```text
A = A1 * A2
99.9% * 99.9% = 99.8%   (worse than either)
```
Chain of services: `Gateway -> Order -> Payment -> DB`. Each dependency **reduces** total availability.

## In parallel (any one is enough)
```text
A = 1 - (1 - A1) * (1 - A2)
1 - (0.001 * 0.001) = 99.9999%
```
Redundant instances behind a load balancer **raise** availability.

## Interview insight
- A request that synchronously calls 5 services at 99.9% each = 99.5% total (~1.8 days/year down).
- Fixes: fewer synchronous hops, async messaging, caching fallbacks, redundancy (parallel) for each tier.

## Example

```java
@CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory", fallbackMethod = "cachedStock")
public Stock stock(Long sku) { return inventoryClient.get(sku); }

Stock cachedStock(Long sku, Throwable t) { return cache.get(sku); }  // degrade, don't fail
```
- A fallback turns a hard sequential dependency into a soft one.

Q: Two 99% services in series, availability?
A: 0.99 * 0.99 = 98.01%. Two in parallel: 1 - 0.01*0.01 = 99.99%.

name: Phase 2 — Building Blocks
description: Components used to build scalable systems
content:
# Phase 2: Building blocks

These are the boxes you draw on the whiteboard: DNS, CDN, load balancer, app servers, databases, caches, queues and the protocols between them. Know **what each does, when to use it, its failure mode, and the Spring Boot equivalent**.

name: Background Jobs
description: Work done outside the request path
content: Move slow or periodic work out of the user's request.

name: Event-Driven
description: Jobs triggered by events such as a message or a file upload

name: Schedule Driven
description: Jobs triggered by time, such as cron
content:
# Schedule-driven background jobs

Run at fixed times or intervals: nightly report, expire old sessions, retry failed payments.

```java
@Component
class ReportJob {
    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *")          // every day 02:00
    @SchedulerLock(name = "dailyReport", lockAtMostFor = "PT30M")   // ShedLock
    void run() { reportService.generate(); }
}
```
- `@EnableScheduling` runs the method on **every instance**. With 3 pods the job runs 3 times. Use **ShedLock** (DB/Redis lock), Quartz clustered mode, or a Kubernetes CronJob so only one runs.

## Options

| Tool | Use when |
|---|---|
| `@Scheduled` + ShedLock | Simple periodic jobs |
| Quartz (JDBC store) | Persistent, clustered, many jobs |
| Kubernetes CronJob | Job as its own container |
| Spring Batch | Large chunked processing with restart |

## Remember
- Make jobs idempotent and restartable; log start/end; alert on failure.

Q: A @Scheduled job fires twice in production. Why?
A: Multiple instances each run the scheduler. Add a distributed lock (ShedLock) or run it as a single CronJob.

name: Returning Results
description: How a client learns the outcome of a background job

name: Domain Name System
description: Turning names into IP addresses
content: How the browser finds your server.

name: DNS
description: Resolution flow, record types, TTL and DNS-based routing
content:
# DNS

DNS maps `api.example.com` → an IP. It is the **phone book** of the internet.

## Resolution flow

```text
Browser cache -> OS cache -> Recursive resolver (ISP / 8.8.8.8)
   -> Root (.) -> TLD (.com) -> Authoritative NS for example.com -> IP
```
Results are cached for the record's **TTL**.

## Record types

| Record | Purpose |
|---|---|
| A / AAAA | Name → IPv4 / IPv6 |
| CNAME | Alias to another name (not allowed at apex) |
| MX | Mail servers |
| NS | Authoritative name servers |
| TXT | Verification, SPF |

## DNS as a design tool
- **Round-robin / weighted:** multiple A records spread load.
- **Latency/geo routing** (Route 53): send users to the nearest region.
- **Failover:** health check removes a dead IP.
- **Trade-off:** low TTL = fast failover but more lookups; high TTL = cached, slow to change.

## Java gotcha: JVM caches DNS

```java
// In a long-lived Spring Boot app behind a changing IP (cloud LB), stale DNS breaks calls.
java.security.Security.setProperty("networkaddress.cache.ttl", "30");
```
- By default the JVM may cache successful lookups for a long time (forever if a SecurityManager is present). Set a short TTL for services behind changing addresses.

Q: What happens when you type a URL?
A: DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request → LB → app → response → render.

name: Content Delivery Networks
description: Serve static content from the edge
content: Move bytes closer to users.

name: Push CDNs
description: You upload content to the CDN ahead of time
content:
# Push CDN

You **push** new/changed files to the CDN yourself. Content sits on edge servers until you remove it.

```text
Deploy -> upload assets to CDN origin storage (S3/GCS) -> replicated to edges
```

## Pros / cons
- (+) Full control, no first-request miss, good for small sites with rare changes.
- (-) You manage uploads and invalidation; wastes storage for rarely used files.

## Use cases
- Versioned build artifacts: `app.3f9a1c.js` (long cache, new name on change).
- Big files released at a known time (game patch, video).

Q: Push vs pull, which for a React build?
A: Push (or deploy to S3 + CDN) with hashed filenames and `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`; only `index.html` is short-lived.

name: Pull CDNs
description: CDN fetches from your origin on first request
content:
# Pull CDN

The CDN **pulls** a file from your origin on the first miss, caches it for the TTL, then serves it from the edge.

```text
User -> Edge (miss) -> Origin (Spring Boot / S3) -> Edge caches -> User
User -> Edge (hit) -> User
```

## Pros / cons
- (+) Easy: just point CDN at origin. Only popular content is cached.
- (-) First request is slow; origin must handle bursts after TTL expiry (use `stale-while-revalidate`).

## Spring Boot: control the cache with headers

```java
@GetMapping("/images/{id}")
ResponseEntity<byte[]> image(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
        .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofDays(7)).cachePublic())
        .eTag(hashOf(id))
        .body(bytes(id));
}
```
- `Cache-Control` tells the CDN and browser how long to keep it; `ETag` allows cheap revalidation (304).

## Remember
- Never cache personalized responses with `public`. Use `Vary` / `private` / `no-store`.

Q: How do you purge a bad file?
A: CDN invalidation API or (better) versioned URLs so the new content has a new URL.

name: Load Balancers
description: Distributing traffic across instances
content: The front door of a scalable service.

name: LB vs Reverse Proxy
description: Both sit in front of servers, with different primary goals
content:
# Load balancer vs reverse proxy

| | Load balancer | Reverse proxy |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | Spread load across many servers | Single entry point for (one or many) servers |
| Features | Health checks, algorithms | TLS termination, caching, compression, auth, routing |
| Examples | AWS ALB/NLB, HAProxy | Nginx, Envoy, API gateway |

In practice **Nginx/Envoy/ALB do both**. The words overlap; explain the *functions*.

```text
Client -> Nginx (TLS, gzip, rate limit) -> [Spring Boot 1, 2, 3]
```

## Forwarded headers in Spring Boot

```yaml
server:
  forward-headers-strategy: framework   # honor X-Forwarded-For / -Proto behind the proxy
```
- Without this the app sees the proxy's IP and `http` instead of the client's IP and `https` (breaks redirects and rate limiting).

Q: Why TLS termination at the proxy?
A: Central certificate management and offloaded CPU; traffic inside the private network can be plain or re-encrypted (mTLS) as needed.

name: Load Balancing Algorithms
description: Round robin, least connections, hash and more
content:
# Load balancing algorithms

| Algorithm | How | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Round robin | Next server in order | Equal servers, short uniform requests |
| Weighted round robin | More requests to bigger servers | Mixed hardware |
| Least connections | Fewest active connections | Long/variable requests |
| IP / consistent hash | Same key → same server | Sticky sessions, cache locality |
| Random (power of two choices) | Pick 2 at random, take the less loaded | Large clusters |

## Sticky sessions: avoid them
- They tie a user to one server; if it dies the session is lost and load becomes uneven.
- Prefer stateless apps (JWT) or shared session store (Spring Session + Redis).

## Client-side load balancing in Spring Cloud

```java
@Bean @LoadBalanced
RestClient.Builder restClient() { return RestClient.builder(); }

restClient.get().uri("http://inventory-service/stock/{id}", id).retrieve()...
```
- Spring Cloud LoadBalancer resolves `inventory-service` via service discovery and round-robins instances **inside the client**, with no central LB.

Q: Which algorithm for WebSocket servers?
A: Least connections (long-lived, uneven load), maybe consistent hashing if you need affinity.

name: Layer 7 Load Balancing
description: Routes by HTTP content (path, header, cookie)
content:
# Layer 7 (application) load balancing

Understands HTTP: it reads the URL, headers, cookies and body metadata, then decides.

```text
/api/orders/**   -> order-service pool
/api/payments/** -> payment-service pool
Host: admin.x.com -> admin pool
```

## Pros / cons
- (+) Smart routing, A/B and canary, TLS termination, WAF, rate limit, caching.
- (-) Slower and more CPU than L4 (it must parse requests, terminate TLS).

## Example: Spring Cloud Gateway as an L7 router

```yaml
spring.cloud.gateway.routes:
  - id: orders
    uri: lb://order-service
    predicates: [ Path=/api/orders/** ]
    filters: [ StripPrefix=0 ]
  - id: canary
    uri: lb://order-service-v2
    predicates: [ Path=/api/orders/**, Weight=orders, 10 ]   # 10% traffic
```

Q: When pick L7 over L4?
A: When routing depends on request content (microservices by path, canary, header-based tenant routing) or you need TLS/WAF.

name: Layer 4 Load Balancing
description: Routes by IP and port (TCP/UDP)
content:
# Layer 4 (transport) load balancing

Looks only at **IP + port**. It forwards TCP/UDP packets without reading HTTP.

## Pros / cons
- (+) Very fast, very high throughput, any protocol (databases, gRPC passthrough, MQTT).
- (-) No content-based routing; cannot cache or inspect.

## Example mapping
- AWS **NLB** = L4 (millions of connections/sec, static IP). AWS **ALB** = L7.
- Use L4 in front of Kafka brokers, database proxies, raw TCP services, or in front of L7 proxies.

```text
Client -> NLB (L4) -> Nginx/Envoy (L7, routing) -> Spring Boot pods
```

Q: L4 or L7 for a gRPC service?
A: L7 that supports HTTP/2 (ALB/Envoy) lets you balance per-request. A plain L4 balances per-connection, and one long HTTP/2 connection can pin all traffic to a single pod.

name: Horizontal Scaling
description: Add more machines, make the app stateless
content:
# Horizontal scaling

Add identical instances behind a load balancer instead of buying a bigger one.

## Requirements
1. **Stateless services:** no user state in memory/local disk.
2. **Shared state externalized:** DB, Redis, object storage.
3. **Idempotent/replay-safe** operations (retries happen).
4. **Auto-scaling** on CPU, RPS or queue depth.

## Spring Boot checklist

| Local (breaks) | Externalize to |
|---|---|
| `HttpSession` | Spring Session + Redis, or JWT |
| In-memory cache | Redis / Caffeine + invalidation |
| Local file uploads | S3 / MinIO |
| `@Scheduled` job | ShedLock / CronJob |
| In-memory ID counter | DB sequence / Snowflake |

```java
@EnableRedisHttpSession    // session now lives in Redis, any pod serves any user
```

## Kubernetes auto-scale (concept)

```yaml
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec: { minReplicas: 3, maxReplicas: 20,
        metrics: [ { type: Resource, resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 } } } ] }
```
- Min 3 across zones means one failure still leaves capacity.

Q: Can you scale the database horizontally like app servers?
A: Not easily. Reads: replicas. Writes: sharding. That is why data is the hard part.

name: Application Layer
description: Service boundaries and discovery
content: Split the app tier and let services find each other.

name: Microservices
description: Small independent services owning their data
content:
# Microservices

An app built as **small services**, each owning one business capability and its **own database**, deployed independently, communicating over the network (REST/gRPC/events).

## Monolith vs microservices

| | Monolith | Microservices |
|---|---|---|
| Deploy | One unit | Per service |
| Scale | Whole app | Per service |
| Complexity | In code | In network/ops |
| Data | One DB, ACID | DB per service, eventual consistency |
| Failure | One bug can kill all | Partial failure, needs resilience |

## Typical Spring Boot stack
- Spring Boot + Spring Cloud Gateway (edge), Eureka/Kubernetes DNS (discovery), Config Server, Resilience4j, Kafka, Micrometer + OpenTelemetry (tracing).

## Interview talking points
- Split by **business domain** (DDD bounded contexts), not by technical layer.
- No shared database between services (otherwise it is a distributed monolith).
- Cross-service transactions → **Saga** (choreography or orchestration), not 2PC.
- Pain: network failure, latency, versioning, debugging → need tracing, timeouts, circuit breakers.

```java
@FeignClient(name = "payment-service", fallback = PaymentFallback.class)
interface PaymentClient { @PostMapping("/payments") PaymentResult pay(PaymentReq r); }
```

Q: When NOT to use microservices?
A: Small team, unclear domain, early product. Start with a modular monolith; extract services when a module needs independent scale/deploy.

name: Service Discovery
description: How services find healthy instances
content:
# Service discovery

IPs change (autoscaling, restarts). Instead of hard-coding, services **register** and clients **look up** by name.

## Two models

| Model | How | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Client-side | Client asks registry, picks an instance | Eureka + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer |
| Server-side | Client calls a stable name; platform routes | Kubernetes Service, AWS ALB |

```text
payment-service (3 pods) --register/heartbeat--> Registry
order-service asks "payment-service" -> [10.0.1.4, 10.0.2.9, 10.0.3.7]
```

## Spring Boot with Eureka

```java
@SpringBootApplication @EnableDiscoveryClient
class PaymentApp {}
```
```yaml
eureka.client.service-url.defaultZone: http://eureka:8761/eureka
```
- On Kubernetes you usually skip Eureka: a `Service` gives a stable DNS name (`http://payment-service`) and kube-proxy balances.

## Remember
- Registries need **health checks + TTL** to evict dead nodes, and are themselves clustered (Consul/etcd/ZooKeeper are CP).

Q: Eureka is AP. What does that imply?
A: During partitions it keeps serving possibly stale registrations (self-preservation mode), so clients must tolerate calling a dead instance: use timeouts and retries.

name: Databases
description: SQL, replication, sharding and data modeling
content: The hardest tier to scale. Know every lever and its cost.

name: SQL vs NoSQL
description: Pick by data shape, consistency and scale needs
content:
# SQL vs NoSQL

| | SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL) | NoSQL (Mongo, Cassandra, Redis, DynamoDB) |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Tables, relations, joins | Key-value, document, wide-column, graph |
| Schema | Fixed, enforced | Flexible |
| Transactions | Full ACID | Often per-record/partition |
| Scale | Vertical + replicas, sharding is manual | Built for horizontal scale |
| Query | Powerful ad-hoc SQL | Designed around known access patterns |

## How to decide
- **Default to PostgreSQL.** It handles most systems up to very large scale (JSONB, full-text, partitioning).
- Choose NoSQL when: massive write throughput, simple access by key, flexible/nested documents, geo-distribution, or a specific model (graph, time-series).
- Often use **both** (polyglot persistence): PostgreSQL for orders, Redis for cache, Elasticsearch for search.

## Spring Data: same app, different stores

```java
interface OrderRepo extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {}           // PostgreSQL
interface SessionRepo extends CrudRepository<Session, String> {}     // Redis
interface ProductDocRepo extends MongoRepository<Product, String> {} // MongoDB
```

## ACID vs BASE
- **ACID:** Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.
- **BASE:** Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent.

Q: "Why not just use MongoDB for everything?"
A: Multi-document transactions, joins and strong constraints are easier and safer in SQL. Use Mongo when the data is genuinely document-shaped with flexible schema.

name: RDBMS
description: ACID, indexes, isolation levels and transactions
content:
# RDBMS essentials

## ACID
- **Atomicity:** all or nothing (rollback).
- **Consistency:** constraints always hold.
- **Isolation:** concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work.
- **Durability:** committed data survives crashes (WAL).

## Isolation levels

| Level | Prevents | Still allows |
|---|---|---|
| Read committed (PG default) | Dirty reads | Non-repeatable, phantom |
| Repeatable read (MySQL default) | + Non-repeatable | Phantom (PG blocks it) |
| Serializable | Everything | Slowest, retries needed |

## Indexes (B-tree)

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);
-- supports: WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC   (leftmost-prefix rule)
```
- Indexes speed reads but slow writes and use space. Index columns in `WHERE`, `JOIN`, `ORDER BY`.

## Spring transaction pitfalls

```java
@Service class A {
    @Transactional public void outer() { inner(); }   // inner() is a plain self-call
    @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void inner() { ... }                       // proxy bypassed: annotation ignored!
}
```
- `@Transactional` works through a **proxy**; self-invocation and `private` methods skip it. Call through another bean.
- Checked exceptions do **not** roll back by default: use `rollbackFor`.

Q: What is a deadlock and how to avoid it?
A: Two transactions wait for each other's locks. Avoid by locking rows in a consistent order, keeping transactions short, and retrying on `DeadlockLoserDataAccessException`.

name: Replication
description: Copy data to more nodes for reads, safety and failover
content:
# Database replication

Keep copies of data on several nodes.

| Mode | Behavior | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronous | Commit waits for replica ack | No data loss, higher write latency |
| Asynchronous | Commit returns immediately | Fast, but lag and possible loss on fail-over |
| Semi-sync | Wait for at least one replica | Balance |

## Purposes
1. **Read scaling** (replicas serve reads).
2. **High availability** (promote a replica).
3. **Backups / analytics** off the primary.

## Monitor lag

```sql
-- PostgreSQL, on the primary
SELECT client_addr, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;
```
- Alert when lag exceeds your tolerance; route sensitive reads to the primary.

## Remember
- Replication scales **reads only**. Write throughput still bounded by a single primary → sharding.
- Replication is not backup: a bad `DELETE` replicates instantly. Keep PITR backups.

Q: How do you scale writes?
A: Vertical scaling, batching/async writes, reduce write amplification (indexes), then shard by a good key.

name: Sharding
description: Split data across databases by a shard key
content:
# Sharding (horizontal partitioning)

Split one big table across **N independent databases**, each holding a subset of rows.

```text
user_id % 4 == 0 -> shard0   |  1 -> shard1  |  2 -> shard2  |  3 -> shard3
```

## Strategies

| Strategy | How | Issue |
|---|---|---|
| Range | `id 1-1M` → shard A | Hot shards (latest range) |
| Hash | `hash(key) % N` | Resharding moves most data |
| Consistent hashing | Ring with virtual nodes | Only ~1/N keys move on change |
| Directory/lookup | Mapping table | Lookup is a bottleneck/SPOF |

## Choosing the shard key (most-asked)
- High cardinality, even distribution, matches the main query (e.g., `user_id` for per-user data).
- Bad: `country` (skew), `created_at` (hot latest shard).

## Spring Boot: routing by tenant/shard

```java
class ShardRouter extends AbstractRoutingDataSource {
    @Override protected Object determineCurrentLookupKey() {
        return "shard" + (ShardContext.userId() % 4);
    }
}
```
- ShardContext is set from the request (e.g., filter). Prefer proven tools (Vitess, Citus, ShardingSphere) over hand-rolled.

## Costs
- Cross-shard joins/transactions are hard or impossible; avoid by modeling per-shard data.
- Resharding is painful; globally unique IDs needed (Snowflake/ULID).
- Hot keys (celebrity user) still overload one shard.

Q: Sharding vs partitioning?
A: Partitioning splits a table inside one DB (e.g., PostgreSQL partitions by month). Sharding spreads data over multiple DB servers.

name: Federation
description: Split databases by function
content:
# Federation (functional partitioning)

Split one database into several **by business function**: users DB, products DB, orders DB.

```text
Before:  one DB (users + products + orders)
After:   users-db | products-db | orders-db   (each with its own load and replicas)
```

## Pros / cons
- (+) Smaller DBs → better cache hit rate, less write contention, independent scaling.
- (-) Cross-database joins need app-level code or API calls; more connections to manage.
- It is the data-side of **microservices** (database per service).

## Spring Boot: multiple DataSources

```java
@Configuration
@EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages = "app.users", entityManagerFactoryRef = "usersEmf",
                       transactionManagerRef = "usersTx")
class UsersDbConfig { /* DataSource + EMF + TxManager for users-db */ }
```
- A `@Transactional` spans only one manager; a transaction cannot cover two DBs without JTA/saga.

Q: Federation or sharding first?
A: Federation is simpler and mirrors service boundaries, so start there. Shard a single domain's table only when it alone outgrows a server.

name: Denormalization
description: Trade write cost and redundancy for faster reads
content:
# Denormalization

Normalized data avoids duplication but needs **joins**. Denormalize by storing redundant data to **avoid joins** on hot read paths.

```text
Normalized:  orders(user_id) JOIN users(name)
Denormalized: orders(user_id, user_name)   // copy name into orders
```

## When
- Read-heavy; joins are the bottleneck; data rarely changes.

## Costs
- Writes must update every copy; risk of inconsistency; more storage.

## Spring/JPA options

```java
@Entity @Immutable
@Subselect("SELECT o.id, u.name FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id")
class OrderView { ... }          // read model

// Or a materialized view in PostgreSQL
// CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW order_summary AS ...;  REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY order_summary;
```
- In **NoSQL** denormalization is the norm: model by query (embed `user` snapshot in the order document).
- Snapshot data that must not change later: order stores the **price at purchase** and address copy, not a reference.

Q: Name a time you should *not* denormalize.
A: Frequently updated values (user name edits) copied to millions of rows; use a join/cache or an event to propagate.

name: SQL Tuning
description: Find slow queries, add the right indexes, fix N+1
content:
# SQL tuning

## Method
1. **Measure:** slow query log, `pg_stat_statements`.
2. **Explain:** `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) ...` → look for `Seq Scan` on big tables.
3. **Fix:** index, rewrite query, reduce data.
4. **Re-measure.**

## High-impact fixes
- Add index matching the filter/sort (composite, leftmost-prefix).
- Avoid `SELECT *`; select only needed columns.
- Avoid functions on indexed columns: `WHERE lower(email)=?` skips the index (use a functional index).
- **Keyset pagination** instead of deep `OFFSET`.
- Batch inserts; use appropriate types.

```sql
-- Slow at page 10,000
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000;
-- Fast (keyset)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT 20;
```

## N+1 problem in JPA (very common question)

```java
List<Order> orders = repo.findAll();             // 1 query
orders.forEach(o -> o.getItems().size());        // +N queries (lazy load per order)

// Fix
@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.items")  // or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")
List<Order> findAllWithItems();
```
- Enable `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics` or p6spy in dev to count queries.

Q: Query is slow although an index exists. Why?
A: The planner may ignore it (low selectivity, type mismatch, function on column, stale stats). Read the plan, run `ANALYZE`, fix the predicate.

name: NoSQL
description: Key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores
content: Each type fits a specific access pattern.

name: Key-Value Store
description: Hash map at scale: get/put by key

name: Document Store
description: JSON documents with flexible schema
content:
# Document store

Stores self-contained JSON/BSON documents, queryable by fields.

**Examples:** MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore.

```json
{ "_id": "o-1001", "user": { "id": 7, "name": "Rahim" },
  "items": [ { "sku": "A1", "qty": 2, "price": 150 } ], "status": "PAID" }
```
- Order + items + user snapshot in **one document** → read with one lookup, no joins.

## Spring Data MongoDB

```java
@Document("orders")
record Order(@Id String id, User user, List<Item> items, String status) {}

interface OrderRepo extends MongoRepository<Order, String> {
    List<Order> findByUserIdAndStatus(long userId, String status);
}
```

## Embed vs reference
- **Embed** when data is read together and bounded in size (items).
- **Reference** when unbounded or shared (comments of a viral post).
- Document size limit (16 MB in Mongo): don't embed unbounded arrays.

Q: Good fit for a document store?
A: Catalogs, content, user profiles, event payloads with varying attributes.

name: Wide Column Store
description: Rows with dynamic columns, partitioned for massive writes
content:
# Wide-column store

Data grouped by **partition key**, sorted by **clustering key** inside a partition. Optimized for huge write volume and time-series.

**Examples:** Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB, Bigtable.

```sql
-- Cassandra: design the table for ONE query
CREATE TABLE messages_by_chat (
  chat_id uuid, sent_at timeuuid, sender text, body text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id), sent_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC);

SELECT * FROM messages_by_chat WHERE chat_id = ? LIMIT 50;   -- latest 50, one partition
```

## Rules
- **Query-first modeling:** one table per query; duplicate data freely.
- No joins; avoid huge partitions (bound with a time bucket: `(chat_id, day)`).
- Tunable consistency (ONE/QUORUM/ALL), write path is LSM-tree (append, very fast).

## Use cases
- Chat history, IoT/telemetry, activity feeds, audit logs.

Q: Why is Cassandra good at writes?
A: Writes go to a commit log and memtable (sequential, in-memory) and are flushed as immutable SSTables; no read-before-write, no in-place update.

name: Graph Databases
description: Nodes and edges for relationship-heavy queries
content:
# Graph databases

Store **nodes** and **relationships**; traversal is cheap (no expensive joins).

**Examples:** Neo4j, Amazon Neptune.

```cypher
// Friends of friends who like the same movie
MATCH (me:User {id: 7})-[:FRIEND]->()-[:FRIEND]->(fof)-[:LIKES]->(m:Movie)<-[:LIKES]-(me)
RETURN DISTINCT fof.name, m.title
```
- The same query in SQL needs several self-joins that explode as depth grows.

## Use cases
- Social networks, recommendations, fraud rings, knowledge graphs, access-control graphs.

## Spring Data Neo4j

```java
@Node class User { @Id Long id; String name; @Relationship("FRIEND") Set<User> friends; }
interface UserRepo extends Neo4jRepository<User, Long> {}
```

Q: When not to use a graph DB?
A: Simple CRUD and aggregates, or when relationships are shallow. Scaling a graph across shards is hard.

name: Types of Caching
description: Where you can cache in the request path
content: Cache at every layer, closest to the user first.

name: Client Caching
description: Browser and mobile cache using HTTP headers

name: CDN Caching
description: Edge caching of static and cacheable API responses
content:
# CDN caching

CDN edge nodes cache responses near users, absorbing most traffic before it reaches your origin.

## What to cache
- Static assets (JS, CSS, images, video).
- Public API responses (`GET /products`, `/config`) with short TTL.

## Key concepts
- **Cache key:** URL + selected headers/query. Normalize to raise hit ratio.
- **TTL & invalidation:** purge by URL/tag or use versioned URLs.
- **Origin shield:** one mid-tier cache to reduce origin hits.
- **`Vary`:** `Vary: Accept-Encoding`; avoid `Vary: Cookie` (kills hit rate).

```java
ResponseEntity.ok()
    .header("Cache-Control", "public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=30")
    .body(catalog);       // CDN (s-maxage) keeps 60s; browser uses default
```
- `s-maxage` targets shared caches (CDN) separately from browsers.

Q: Metric to watch?
A: **Cache hit ratio** (>90% for static); and origin offload.

name: Web Server Caching
description: Reverse-proxy cache (Nginx, Varnish) in front of the app

name: Database Caching
description: DB buffer cache, query cache and tuning
content:
# Database caching

The database already caches internally.

- **Buffer pool / shared_buffers:** hot data pages stay in RAM. Fit the working set in memory.
- **Query plan cache / prepared statements:** parse and plan once.
- **MySQL query cache** was removed (8.0): invalidation cost outweighed benefit.
- **Materialized views:** precomputed results.

## Tuning actions
- Enough RAM for the working set, right `shared_buffers`/`innodb_buffer_pool_size`.
- Use **prepared statements** and a connection pool.

```yaml
spring.datasource.hikari:
  maximum-pool-size: 20
  data-source-properties:
    prepStmtCacheSize: 250       # MySQL driver prepared-statement cache
    cachePrepStmts: true
```

## Hibernate second-level cache
- L1 = per `EntityManager` (always on). L2 = shared across sessions (Ehcache/Hazelcast/Redis); good for read-mostly reference data.
```java
@Entity @Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_ONLY) class Country { ... }
```

Q: When is L2 cache dangerous?
A: With multiple app instances and writes: stale data unless the cache is distributed/invalidated. Use it only for read-mostly data.

name: Application Caching
description: In-process (Caffeine) and distributed (Redis) caches

name: Caching Strategies
description: How data enters and leaves the cache
content: Read and write patterns.

name: Cache Aside
description: App checks cache first, loads from DB on miss

name: Write-through
description: Write to cache and DB together synchronously
content:
# Write-through

Every write goes to the **cache and DB synchronously**; reads always hit a warm cache.

```text
write -> cache (update) -> DB (update) -> ack
read  -> cache (always populated)
```

## Pros / cons
- (+) Cache never stale for written data; fast reads.
- (-) Higher write latency (two writes); caches data that may never be read.

## Spring example

```java
@CachePut(value = "product", key = "#p.id")   // write-through-like: always refresh cache
@Transactional
public Product save(Product p) { return repo.save(p); }
```
- Combine with cache-aside for reads. Good for read-heavy data where freshness matters (profiles).

Q: Write-through failure case?
A: Cache updated but DB write fails (or reverse) → inconsistency. Order the operations and handle rollback, or let the cache provider do the DB write.

name: Write-behind
description: Write to cache, flush to DB asynchronously
content:
# Write-behind (write-back)

Write to cache, ack quickly, and **flush to DB later in batches**.

```text
write -> cache -> ack
          \-> queue -> batch flush to DB every N sec
```

## Pros / cons
- (+) Very fast writes, batching reduces DB load, absorbs spikes.
- (-) **Data loss** if the cache dies before the flush; eventual consistency; complex.

## Use cases
- Counters (views, likes), telemetry, where small loss is OK.

```java
// view counter: increment in Redis, flush periodically
redis.opsForValue().increment("views:" + postId);

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5000)
void flush() { /* read-and-reset counters, then UPDATE posts SET views = views + :n */ }
```
- For must-not-lose data use a durable log (Kafka) as the buffer instead of memory.

Q: Why not write-behind for payments?
A: Acknowledged but unsaved data can be lost. Payments need durable synchronous writes.

name: Refresh Ahead
description: Reload hot entries before they expire
content:
# Refresh-ahead

Predict which keys will be requested and **refresh them just before TTL expiry** so users never see a miss.

```text
TTL = 10 min. When a hit happens after minute 8 -> async reload in background; return current value.
```

## Pros / cons
- (+) Low read latency, avoids stampede on hot keys.
- (-) Needs good prediction; wasted refreshes on keys no longer used.

## Caffeine support

```java
Caffeine.newBuilder()
    .expireAfterWrite(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
    .refreshAfterWrite(8, TimeUnit.MINUTES)       // async reload, serves old value meanwhile
    .build(key -> loadFromDb(key));               // LoadingCache
```
- `refreshAfterWrite` returns the stale value instantly and reloads on a background thread.

Q: Refresh-ahead vs cache-aside?
A: Cache-aside loads on a miss (user waits). Refresh-ahead loads before the miss, ideal for a small set of very hot keys.

name: Asynchronism
description: Queues and decoupling
content: Do slow work later, smooth bursts.

name: Message Queues
description: Producers and consumers decoupled by a broker
content:
# Message queues

A broker stores messages; producers don't wait for consumers.

```text
Order API --publish--> [ Kafka / RabbitMQ ] --consume--> Email / Inventory / Analytics
```

## Why
- **Decoupling**, **buffering spikes**, **retry**, **fan-out**, independent scaling.

## RabbitMQ vs Kafka

| | RabbitMQ | Kafka |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Smart broker, queues, routing | Distributed append-only log |
| Delivery | Push, message removed after ack | Pull, retained; consumers track offset |
| Ordering | Per queue | Per partition |
| Best for | Task queues, complex routing | High-throughput streams, replay, event sourcing |

## Spring Boot Kafka

```java
@Service class Publisher {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> kafka;
    void send(OrderPlaced e) { kafka.send("orders", e.orderId(), e); }    // key => same partition => ordered per order
}

@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "inventory", concurrency = "3")
void on(OrderPlaced e) { inventory.reserve(e); }
```

## Delivery semantics
- At-most-once, **at-least-once (default, need idempotent consumers)**, exactly-once (Kafka transactions, limited scope).
- Failed messages → retry with backoff → **dead-letter topic (DLT)**.

Q: How to keep order in Kafka?
A: Use the same key so messages land in the same partition; one consumer per partition in a group.

name: Task Queues
description: Background job processing with workers

name: Back Pressure
description: Slow down or reject producers when consumers are overloaded
content:
# Back pressure

If producers are faster than consumers, queues grow without bound → memory exhaustion and huge latency. Back pressure **pushes the overload back** to the producer.

## Techniques
- **Bounded queues** that block or reject (return `503`/`429`).
- **Rate limiting** at the gateway.
- **Load shedding:** drop low-priority work.
- Consumers **pull** at their own pace (Kafka polling) and scale out by lag.
- Reactive streams (`Flux`) with demand signalling.

```java
// Reactor: consumer controls the rate
Flux.range(1, 1_000_000)
    .onBackpressureBuffer(1_000, dropped -> log.warn("dropped"))
    .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())
    .subscribe(this::process, e -> {}, () -> {}, s -> s.request(10));

// Servlet: reject when saturated
if (!executor.getThreadPoolExecutor().getQueue().offer(task)) throw new ResponseStatusException(TOO_MANY_REQUESTS);
```
- Autoscale consumers on **consumer lag** (KEDA with Kafka).

Q: Queue depth keeps growing. What do you do?
A: Add consumers (up to partition count), speed up processing, apply back pressure/rate limit producers, and shed or defer low-priority work.

name: Idempotent Operations
description: Repeating a request has the same effect as doing it once

name: Communication
description: Protocols and API styles
content: How components talk.

name: HTTP
description: Request/response protocol, methods, status codes, versions
content:
# HTTP

Stateless request-response protocol over TCP (HTTP/3 over QUIC).

## Methods

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | yes | yes | Read |
| POST | no | no | Create / action |
| PUT | no | yes | Replace |
| PATCH | no | no* | Partial update |
| DELETE | no | yes | Remove |

## Status codes
`200` OK, `201` Created, `204` No content, `301/302` redirect, `304` Not modified, `400` bad request, `401` unauthenticated, `403` forbidden, `404`, `409` conflict, `429` too many requests, `500` server error, `502/503/504` gateway/unavailable/timeout.

## Versions
- **1.1:** keep-alive, one request at a time per connection (head-of-line blocking).
- **2:** multiplexing, header compression, binary.
- **3:** QUIC/UDP, no TCP head-of-line blocking.

## Spring Boot client with timeouts (always set them)

```java
RestClient client = RestClient.builder()
    .requestFactory(new JdkClientHttpRequestFactory(
        HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build()))
    .build();
```
- Missing timeouts are the #1 cause of cascading failures: threads block forever on a slow dependency.

Q: 401 vs 403?
A: 401 = not authenticated (who are you?). 403 = authenticated but not allowed.

name: TCP
description: Reliable, ordered, connection-oriented transport
content:
# TCP

Guarantees **ordered, reliable** delivery via handshake, sequence numbers, acks, retransmission, flow and congestion control.

```text
Client SYN ->  <- SYN-ACK  Client ACK ->     (3-way handshake, 1 RTT)
... data ...
FIN / ACK ... (close)
```

## Costs
- Handshake latency (plus TLS), head-of-line blocking on loss, slow start.
- Mitigate: **connection pooling / keep-alive**, HTTP/2.

## Why it matters in Java
- Opening a connection per request is expensive → use pooled clients (Hikari for DB, Apache/Reactor Netty client pools).

```yaml
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 20
```
- `TIME_WAIT` exhaustion at high rates happens when connections are not reused.

Q: Why TCP for payments but UDP for video calls?
A: Payments need every byte correct and ordered. Calls prefer low latency; a late packet is useless, so retransmission is wasted.

name: UDP
description: Connectionless, low-latency, no delivery guarantee
content:
# UDP

Sends datagrams with **no handshake, no ordering, no retransmission**. Lower overhead and latency.

**Used by:** DNS, video/voice (WebRTC), gaming, metrics (StatsD), QUIC/HTTP3 (reliability built on top).

| | TCP | UDP |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | Yes | No |
| Reliable / ordered | Yes | No |
| Overhead | Higher | Lower |
| Broadcast/multicast | No | Yes |

## Java sketch

```java
try (DatagramSocket socket = new DatagramSocket()) {
    byte[] data = "metric:1|c".getBytes(UTF_8);
    socket.send(new DatagramPacket(data, data.length, InetAddress.getByName("statsd"), 8125));
}
```
- Fire-and-forget: acceptable to lose an occasional metric.

Q: Is UDP "unreliable"?
A: It gives no guarantee; the application adds reliability if needed (QUIC does it in user space).

name: REST
description: Resource-oriented APIs over HTTP

name: RPC
description: Call a remote function like a local one
content:
# RPC (Remote Procedure Call)

The client calls `paymentService.charge(req)` and a framework turns it into a network call (serialize, send, deserialize). Action-oriented, not resource-oriented.

**Examples:** gRPC, Thrift, JSON-RPC, Java RMI (legacy).

## RPC vs REST

| | RPC | REST |
|---|---|---|
| Style | Verbs/methods | Resources |
| Coupling | Tighter (shared contract/stubs) | Looser |
| Performance | Binary, fast | Text JSON |
| Use | Internal service-to-service | Public APIs |

## The big warning
"Network calls look like local calls but are not": latency, failure, partial success. Always add **timeouts, retries (idempotent only), circuit breakers**.

```java
@FeignClient(name = "inventory", url = "${inventory.url}")
interface InventoryClient { @GetMapping("/stock/{sku}") Stock stock(@PathVariable String sku); }  // declarative RPC-ish
```

Q: Why internal RPC and public REST?
A: RPC is efficient and typed for internal calls you control; REST is universal and easy for third parties.
